newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to decide on new Bank of France members.
newsitem.headline: France to decide on new Bank of France members.

text.p: The French government is expected on Friday to name two members of the Bank of France's policy-making body in what will be President Jacques Chirac's first real chance since his 1995 election to influence monetary policy.

Officials at Chirac's office have refused comment on the replacement of two members of the nine-member monetary policy council (CPM), ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat and former banker Bruno de Maulde, whose mandates expire next week.

But one source close to the nomination process said the government could choose Pierre Guillen, ex-head of the CNPF employers' association, and Jean-Rene Bernard, former deputy governor of property lender Credit Foncier.
The newspaper Le Monde said last week the Bank of France, which gives an opinion in a purely advisory capacity, had recommended Boissonnat, who is seeking to stay on, and Bernard.

Other sources had said previously that Chirac had intervened personally to get Guillen and Bernard on the list of six nominees proposed by the heads of the upper and lower houses of parliament and the Economic and Social Council.
The names of the two members are expected to be announced on Friday after a cabinet meeting.
Financial markets are watching the decision closely for any sign of a softening in the bank's traditionally cautious approach to monetary easing.

Boissonnat and de Maulde are believed to be part of a six to three majority backing the existing policy of maintaining interest rates slightly above those in Germany to keep the franc stable against the mark.

Two others members have argued publicly that France should cut rates without waiting for a German easing to revive the economy and help bring down record 12.7 percent unemployment. A third member is believed to share that view.
The replacement of Boissonnat and de Maulde by two more dovish members could tip the balance in their favour.

Bank of France Governor Jean-Claude Trichet, mindful of a 1993 attempt to bring French rates below German rates that ended in a franc crisis, is believed to oppose trying to do this again as long as the franc is below its European Exchange Rate Mechanism central rate of 3.35 per mark.
The franc traded on Thursday at 3.3720/24 per mark.

Whatever Friday's decision, Chirac, who has repeatedly stated his commitment to a stable currency, is seen as unlikely to do anything to endanger the franc-mark link, the cornerstone of the future European single currency.
So if Chirac named Guillen and Bernard, it would probably be on the understanding no risks were to be taken with the franc.

"If he (Chirac) were to change the policy at the Bank of France, it would be to change his policy on Europe and I don't think he is going to do that," Societe Generale economist Michala Marcussen said.
The nomination of Guillen and Bernard, and ousting of Boissonnat, a vocal supporter of the stable franc policy, would nonetheless give Chirac big leverage over the Bank of France.
"If it is Guillen and Bernard that would mean Chirac has succeeded in getting the CPM under his control," one political observer commented.
In an interview with Reuters last month Guillen said he was "radically against" devaluing the franc, but as an industrialist would have liked to have seen rates come down faster.

Bernard, whose son-in-law is deputy secretary-general in Chirac's office, is not thought to have very strong convictions on monetary policy. But he is close to Chirac and would be expected to follow the president on policy.

The other candidates on the list of nominees are diplomat Pierre Achard, Alain Prate, former vice-president of the European Investment Bank (EIB), and Robert Pelletier, former managing director of the Association of Credit Establishments (Afec), sources close to the nomination process have said.
